# The Country of Night

In January 1994, an earthquake struck Los Angeles in the dark hours of the morning and knocked out power across most of the city. Residents came out of their houses and looked up at a sky none of them recognized, and some of them called 911, and some called the Griffith Observatory, to ask about an enormous, ominous, silvery cloud hanging over the streets. The cloud was the Milky Way. Many of the callers had lived their entire lives beneath it without once seeing it.

I think about those phone calls often. They hold a parable in miniature. We have altered the night so thoroughly, and so quickly, that most of us have forgotten what it is — have gone, in a historical eyeblink, from being creatures of the dark to creatures who visit the dark, briefly, through a window. Night is half of everything. The Earth spends half of every rotation turned away from the sun, and for all but the last century of our species' existence, we spent that half in a darkness modern people have never once experienced. What follows is an attempt to remember what that half was like: what the night used to be, what we built in its place, and what — this is the hopeful part — is still recoverable, with a switch.

Begin with the basics. For almost the entire human story, night was genuinely dark. Not dim — dark. There was no glow on the horizon from a town over the hill, because there was no glow. Under a new moon in open country you could not see your hand in front of your face. Travelers got lost between villages a mile apart. The moon was the only streetlamp, and it kept an eccentric schedule. Light was the exception and the expense — expensive in treasure, expensive in danger, since keeping flame alive inside a house of thatch and timber was always a small gamble with everyone's life.

Because night was genuinely dangerous, our ancestors organized against it. The word *curfew* comes from the French *couvre-feu*: cover the fire. In medieval towns a bell rang at a fixed hour ordering every hearth banked — a city of wooden roofs collectively exhaling its flames so it could sleep without burning down. In London you could hire a link-boy, a child with a flaming torch, to walk you home through streets that had no public light at all. The night had its own jurisdiction. Thieves and smugglers used it; so did ghosts, demons, and the restless dead; folklore assigned the hours after midnight to spirits and the hours before dawn to melancholy. Darkness wasn't an aesthetic. It was a weather system, and people dressed for it.

Yet the historians of night keep returning to something else: the darkness was also furnished with intimacy. Families slept in shared beds for warmth, packed in with visitors and apprentices and strangers off the road. Conversation in the dark has a candor daylight doesn't allow — when nobody can see anyone, something loosens. Firelight was the gathering point; storytelling was the entertainment; the night functioned less as the day's enemy than as its annex, a second room in the house of the world.

There is an economic way to see how recently all this changed. An economist named William Nordhaus once spent years doing something that sounds absurd and turned out to be illuminating in both senses: pricing light across history. His finding, roughly: for most of human history, an hour of reading by lamp cost the better part of a day's wage. In some ancient reckonings, an hour of oil-lamp light cost days of labor. Today an hour of electric light costs a fraction of a second of median earnings. When you hear that darkness ruled most of human life, understand it as a matter of budget. The night reigned because light was unaffordable. We did not so much abolish the night as make it cheap to ignore.

In 2005, the historian Roger Ekirch published *At Day's Close*, a history of night in the pre-industrial West, built from years spent in diaries, letters, court records, sermons, and medical texts. Reading through them, he kept tripping over a phrase: *first sleep*. It appears in English, in French (*premier sommeil*), in Italian (*primo sonno*), across two millennia, always in the tone people use for things that everyone knows. First sleep was the sleep you took when you went to bed not long after dark. You slept hard, deeply, for three or four hours. Then, around midnight, you woke — not with a jolt, but naturally, gently, into a calm interlude that contemporaries called *the watch*, which might last an hour or more.

People did things in the watch. They got up and tended the fire, prayed, talked, smoked a pipe, checked on the livestock, gossiped with neighbors who were also awake, made love — the physicians of the era actually recommended the interval as the best time for conception — or simply lay still and thought, with no daylight errands left to dilute the thinking. Then they went back down into second sleep until dawn.

For a long time this looked like mere custom. Then in the 1990s, Thomas Wehr, a sleep researcher at the National Institute of Mental Health, ran what amounted to an attempt to retrieve the old night in a laboratory. He gave volunteers fourteen hours of darkness each night for a month — a clinical winter. After an adjustment period, the subjects did something remarkable: their sleep split. They slept in two blocks, waking after midnight into a quiet, dreamy, distinctly pleasant wakefulness — prolactin rising, the body settling into a mode no one had a name for — and then slept again until morning. The pattern Ekirch had found in five centuries of documents reappeared the moment darkness was returned to it. Bimodal sleep looks less like a habit we once had and more like a setting we lost.

Which casts a strange, tender light on a modern complaint. Waking at 3 a.m. and finding ourselves awake, unable to sink back down, we call it insomnia and treat it as a malfunction. It may be an echo — the watch arriving punctually in a world no longer shaped to receive it. The hour may not be broken. The schedule around it is.

The machines that ended the night arrived fast. Gaslight appeared on London's Pall Mall in 1807; within a few decades, tens of thousands of burners glowed in London and Paris, and the lamplighter with his long pole became a fixture of dusk — a moving constellation at eye level. Then came electricity: arc lamps like small captive suns in the 1870s and 80s, then Edison's filaments. By 1900, the night — the oldest human condition, older than language, older than fire's domestication — had been converted into an infrastructure problem with a solution.

What artificial light actually invented was the evening. Before it, the hours after dark belonged to rest, talk, and courtship by candle. After it, they became a market: theaters, cafés, dance halls, cinemas, restaurants, the glittering secondary life of cities that now runs from seven at night until two in the morning. The city that never sleeps stopped being a boast and became a specification.

The cost was absorbed by a workforce most of us never see. Walk through any city at four in the morning and you will find it inhabited: bakers shaping loaves in yellow light, nurses on their rounds, stocking crews wheeling pallets, controllers watching blips, the technicians who keep the water pumping and the servers humming, drivers on their second coffee. Millions of people — in industrialized countries, as many as one in five workers — labor while the rest of us sleep, an invisible crew our comfort floats on. In 2007, the World Health Organization's cancer research agency did something quiet and remarkable: it classified shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable human carcinogen. Night, once merely frightening, now has a mortality schedule.

And then there is the sky itself. In 2016, an international team led by the physicist Fabio Falchi published the first complete atlas of artificial sky brightness. Its numbers deserve to be sat with for a moment. More than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. For a third of humanity, the Milky Way is invisible. In Europe, roughly 60 percent of people cannot see it; in North America, about 80 percent cannot. Look at the Earth from orbit at night — NASA's composite images render civilization as a lace of light strung along coastlines and rivers — and you are looking at something genuinely beautiful that is also, in a sense, exhaust: light escaping upward, scattering off the atmosphere into a luminous dome, a *skyglow* detectable from a hundred miles away.

Living things swim in that exhaust. For centuries, "like a moth to a flame" implied desire. Slow-motion cameras have shown something stranger: insects instinctively tilt their backs toward the brightest point in view, a reflex calibrated to keep them upright beneath an open sky with the moon as a steady reference overhead. Around a porch light, the reflex becomes a doom-loop. They circle not because they love the light but because their bodies are convinced it is the sky.

Migrating birds steer by starlight and the earth's glow, and city lights pull them off course; collisions with buildings kill as many as a billion birds a year in the United States. The Tribute in Light over Manhattan after September 11 — two towers of pure vertical brightness — turned out to be an accidental experiment: migrating birds gathered in orbit inside the beams at extraordinary densities, and when researchers persuaded the organizers to douse the lights for twenty minutes, the birds dispersed almost immediately. The machinery of their confusion simply switched off. Sea turtle hatchlings, emerging at night on a beach, orient toward the brighter horizon — on a wild coast that is moonlight on water; on a developed one, it is a resort — and Florida towns now pass lighting ordinances every hatching season so that hatchlings find the ocean instead of the parking lot. Even plants feel it: a Swiss study found that meadow plots lit by ordinary LED lamps at night received nearly two-thirds fewer visits from pollinating insects, and set less fruit. Night is not empty. Darkness is not the absence of habitat; it *is* habitat, for a vast fraction of the living world, and we have been paving it the way we pave wetlands — without quite noticing, because it doesn't look like anything.

And what of the mind in all this? The 3 a.m. brain has its reputation for a reason. Partly it is mechanics: the prefrontal cortex is tired, no news arrives, no errands interrupt, no one is awake to reality-check you, and rumination gets the whole room. Anxieties that daylight dilutes concentrate in the dark like sediment in a glass. Every insomniac knows the special physics of the 3 a.m. problem: it is always larger at night, and by morning it has shrunk back to size, as though daylight were a solvent.

But night also does stranger, kinder work. Mary Shelley was eighteen in 1816, the year without a summer, holed up on Lake Geneva with Byron and a dare to write ghost stories, when she fell into what she called a waking dream — the pale student, the thing stirring on the table — that became *Frankenstein*. Kekulé claimed the ring structure of benzene came to him as a dream of a snake seizing its own tail. The unconscious keeps the night shift. It takes the problems we fall asleep holding and returns them rearranged by morning. Night thought is not defective day thought; it is a different instrument — looser, less defended — and some of what our species has made appeared first in that other room.

Here is the good news, and it is rare enough in environmental news of any kind: this particular damage reverses at the speed of a switch. Air and water pollution take decades and fortunes to undo. Light pollution ends when the light ends. The dark-sky movement has mapped this out in practice. Central Idaho holds a certified dark sky reserve the size of a small country. On the Isle of Coll, off Scotland, an entire community agreed to manage its lighting so that visitors can see the Milky Way from the football pitch. Tucson, Arizona, sits within sight of some of the world's great observatories, and decades ago the city rewrote its lighting code — full shielding, warm bulbs, light aimed at the ground where it is useful instead of the sky where it isn't — and the observatories kept their view. None of these places is poorer for it. They simply buy their light the way our ancestors had to: on purpose.

And at the scale of a single evening: it takes about twenty minutes of true darkness for human eyes to reach full sensitivity — a dilation you can feel happening, the world quietly assembling itself out of fainter and fainter signals. Guides at dark-sky parks report a curious thing: visitors who see the Milky Way for the first time go silent, and some of them weep. Not only, I think, at the beauty of it — a river of several hundred billion suns, visible to the naked eye — but at the return of something. Gratitude and grief feel similar at first.

Which brings us back to Los Angeles in 1994. The silvery cloud over the blacked-out city had been there the whole time — above the traffic, above the billboards, the whole time. It took a catastrophe to show people what they had, in effect, turned off. There is a version of that blackout available in miniature, any night, anywhere. Our ancestors woke in the watch and lay in the dark between first sleep and second sleep, unbothered, watching embers, thinking their long thoughts, sometimes stepping outside into a sky absolutely stiff with stars. Some of us still wake in that hour and reach, first thing, for a small bright screen — colonizing the last of the night even from bed. But the wakefulness might be read another way: not as a malfunction, but as punctuality. The night was never the other half of the world. It is the half we came from, and it is still there, patient, just above the streetlights, waiting for the switch.

**The Country of Night**

In January 1994, an earthquake struck Los Angeles in the dark hours of the morning and knocked out power across the city. Residents came out of their houses and looked up at a sky none of them recognized, and some of them called 911, and some called the Griffith Observatory, to ask about an enormous, ominous, silvery cloud hanging over the streets. The cloud was the Milky Way. Many of the callers had lived their entire lives beneath it without once seeing it.

I think about those phone calls often. They hold a parable in miniature. We have altered the night so thoroughly, and so quickly, that most of us have forgotten what it is — have gone, in a historical eyeblink, from being creatures of the dark to creatures who visit the dark, briefly, through a window. Night is half of everything. The Earth spends half of every rotation turned away from the sun, and for all but the last hundred-odd years of our species' existence, we spent that half in a darkness modern people have never experienced. What follows is an attempt to remember what that half was like: what the night used to be, what we built in its place, and what — this is the hopeful part — is still recoverable, with a switch.

[The old night]

Begin with the basics: for almost the entire human story, night was genuinely dark. Not dim. Dark. No light pollution existed... Under a new moon in open country you could not see your hand in front of your face. Travelers got lost between villages a mile apart; the moon was the only streetlamp and it kept an eccentric schedule. Light was the exception and the expense — expensive in treasure, expensive in danger. Burning flame inside a house of thatch and timber was always a small gamble.

Because night was genuinely dangerous, our ancestors organized against it. The word curfew comes from the French couvre-feu: cover the fire. In medieval towns a bell rang at a fixed hour ordering every hearth banked — a city of wooden roofs collectively exhaling its flames so everyone could sleep without the town burning down. In cities like London you could hire a link-boy, a child with a flaming torch, to walk you home through streets with no public light at all. The night had its own jurisdiction. Thieves, smugglers, and worse used it; so did the feared dead; folklore assigned the hours after midnight to spirits and the hours before dawn to melancholy.

And yet — this is what the historians emphasize — the darkness was also furnished with intimacy. Families slept in shared beds for warmth, packed like spoons with visitors and apprentices and travelers; conversation in the dark has a candor daylight doesn't allow... Firelight and storytelling; the night as the day's annex rather than its enemy.

There's an economic way to see how recently all this changed. William Nordhaus (economist who spent a career pricing light): for most of history an hour of reading by lamp cost the better part of a day's wage — in some ancient accounting, days of labor for an hour of oil-lamp light. Today an hour of electric light costs a fraction of a second of median earnings. When you hear that darkness covered most of human life, understand it as a matter of budget: the night ruled because light was unaffordable. We didn't abolish night so much as make it cheap to ignore.

[First sleep]

In 2005, the historian Roger Ekirch published "At Day's Close," a history of night in the pre-industrial West, built from years of reading diaries, letters, court records, medical texts, sermons. Reading it, you notice him tripping over the same phrase again and again: "first sleep." It appears in English, in French (premier sommeil), in Italian (primo sonno), across two millennia, always in the tone people use for things everyone knows. First sleep was the sleep you took when you went to bed not long after dark. You slept hard, deeply, for three or four hours; then around midnight you woke — not with a start but naturally, into a calm interlude that contemporaries called the watch — which might last an hour or more.

People did things in the watch. They got up and tended the fire, prayed, talked, made love — physicians of the era recommended the interval as the best time for conception — smoked a pipe, gossiped with neighbors who were also awake, checked on livestock, or simply lay still and thought, with no daylight errands to dilute the thinking. Then they went back down into second sleep until dawn.

For a long time this looked like custom. Then in the 1990s, Thomas Wehr, a sleep researcher at the National Institute of Mental Health, ran what amounted to an experiment in retrieving the old night: he gave volunteers fourteen hours of darkness each night for a month — a laboratory version of a winter. After an adjustment period, the subjects did something remarkable. Their sleep split. They slept in two blocks, waking after midnight into a quiet, dreamy, distinctly pleasant wakefulness — prolactin rising, the body in a mode no one had a name for — then slept again until "morning." The pattern Ekirch had found in five centuries of documents appeared in a lab when darkness was returned. Bimodal sleep looks less like a habit we had and more like a setting we lost.

Which casts a strange light on a modern complaint. Waking at 3 a.m., unable to return to sleep, we call it insomnia, a malfunction. It may be an echo — the watch arriving punctually in a world no longer shaped to receive it. The hour itself may not be broken. The schedule around it is.

[The conquest]

The machines that ended the night arrived quickly... Gaslight: Pall Mall in 1807; within decades, tens of thousands of burners in London and Paris, and the lamplighter with his pole became a fixture of dusk, a moving constellation at eye level. Then electricity: arc lamps like small captive suns in the 1870s-80s, then Edison's bulbs. By 1900 night, the oldest human condition, had become an infrastructure problem with a solution.

What artificial light actually invented was the evening. Before it, the hours after dark belonged to rest, talk, and courtship by candle; after it, they became a market: theaters, cafés, dance halls, cinemas, restaurants, the whole glittering secondary life of cities that now runs from 7 p.m. to 2 a.m. The city that never sleeps stopped being a boast and became a specification.

The cost was absorbed by a workforce most of us never see. Walk through any city at 4 a.m. and you will find it inhabited: bakers shaping loaves, nurses on their fourth round, stocking crews, controllers watching blips, technicians keeping water pumping and servers humming, drivers. Something like a fifth of workers in industrial countries now work nights. In 2007 the WHO's cancer research agency did something quiet and remarkable: it classified shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable human carcinogen — a formal acknowledgment that working against the body's ancient clock exacts a measurable tax. Night, once merely frightening, now has a mortality schedule.

[What we did to the sky]

Then the sky itself. In 2016, an international team led by Fabio Falchi published the first complete atlas of artificial sky brightness. Its numbers are worth sitting with: more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. For a third of humanity, the Milky Way is invisible. In Europe about 60 percent of people, and in North America about 80 percent, cannot see the galaxy they live inside.

Look at Earth from orbit at night — NASA's composite images — and you see civilization as a lace of light strung along coastlines and rivers. It's genuinely beautiful, and it is the exhaust of what we did: light escaping upward, scattering off the atmosphere into a luminous dome — skyglow — that can be detected a hundred miles from the nearest town.

Animals live inside that exhaust. Moths... For centuries the saying "like a moth to a flame" implied attraction. Slow-motion cameras have shown something stranger: insects instinctively tilt their backs toward the brightest point in view — a reflex calibrated to keep them upright beneath an open sky, with the moon overhead as a steady reference. Around a porch light, the reflex turns into a doom-loop; they circle not because they love the light but because their bodies are convinced it is the sky.

Birds: hundreds of species migrate at night, steering by stars and the earth's glow, and city lights pull them off course — collisions with buildings kill as many as a billion birds a year in the United States. A famous experiment in accidental astronomy: the 9/11 Tribute in Light in Manhattan drew migrating birds into orbit inside the beams at enormous rates; researchers persuaded the organizers to douse the lights for twenty minutes, and the birds dispersed almost immediately — the machinery of their confusion simply switched off.

Sea turtles: hatchlings emerge at night and orient toward the brighter horizon — on a wild beach, moonlight and starlight on water; on a developed one, a resort. Towns in Florida now pass beach lighting ordinances each hatching season, dimming and shielding lights so hatchlings can find the ocean instead of the parking lot. Plants, too: a Swiss study found that meadow plots lit at night by ordinary LED lamps received nearly two-thirds fewer visits from pollinating insects — and the plants set less fruit. Night is not empty. Darkness is not the absence of habitat; it is habitat, for a large fraction of the living world, and we have been paving it the way we pave wetlands, without noticing, because it doesn't look like anything.

[The night mind]

And us. Why does 3 a.m. have its reputation? Partly mechanics: the prefrontal cortex is tired, no news arrives, no errands interrupt, no one is awake to reality-check you; rumination gets the whole room. Anxieties that daylight dilutes concentrate in the dark like sediment in a glass. Every insomniac knows the special physics of the 3 a.m. problem: it is always larger at night, and by morning it has shrunk back to size, as though daylight were a solvent.

But night also does stranger and kinder work. Mary Shelley was eighteen in 1816, the year without a summer, holed up on Lake Geneva with Byron and her husband and ghost stories by candlelight, when she described falling into a waking dream — the pale student, the thing stirring on the table — that became Frankenstein. Kekulé claimed the structure of benzene arrived in a dream of a snake seizing its own tail. (Maybe.) The unconscious keeps the night shift; it takes the problems we fall asleep on and returns them rearranged. Night thought is not defective day thought. It is a different instrument — looser, less defended — and some of what our species has made appeared first in that other room.

[Taking the night back]

Here is the good news, and it is rare in environmental news of any kind: this particular damage reverses at the speed of a switch. Air and water pollution take decades and fortune to undo; light pollution ends when the light ends. The dark-sky movement — DarkSky International and its certified places — has mapped this out in practice. Central Idaho contains a certified dark sky reserve the size of a small country. On the Isle of Coll, off Scotland, the whole community agreed to manage its lighting so visitors can see the Milky Way from a football pitch. Tucson, Arizona, sits near some of the great observatories in the world, and decades ago the city rewrote its lighting code — full shielding, warm bulbs, light pointed at the ground where it's useful instead of the sky where it isn't — and the observatories kept their view. None of these places is poorer or darker for it; they simply buy their light the way earlier generations had to, on purpose.

And at personal scale: it takes about twenty minutes of true darkness for human eyes to reach full sensitivity — a dilation you can feel happening, the world slowly assembling itself out of fainter and fainter signals. Guides at dark-sky parks report a curious thing: visitors who see the Milky Way for the first time go quiet, and some of them cry. Not only, I think, at the beauty — a river of several hundred billion suns visible to the naked eye — but at the return of something. Grief and gratitude feel similar at first.

Which brings us back to Los Angeles in 1994. The silvery cloud over the blacked-out city had been there the whole time, above the traffic and the billboards, the whole time. It took a catastrophe to show people what they had, in effect, turned off — or rather, what they still had and couldn't see. There is a version of that blackout available in miniature. Our ancestors woke in the watch and lay in the dark between first sleep and second sleep, unbothered, watching embers, thinking their long thoughts, sometimes stepping outside into a sky absolutely stiff with stars. Some of us still wake in that hour and reach, first thing, for a small bright screen — colonizing the last of the night even from bed. The invitation misdelivered might be read another way. It is the half we came from, and it is still there, patient, just above the streetlights, waiting for the switch.

**The Country of Night**

In January 1994, an earthquake struck Los Angeles in the dark hours of the morning and knocked out power across the city. Residents came out of their houses and looked up at a sky none of them recognized, and some of them called 911, and some called the Griffith Observatory, to ask about an enormous, ominous, silvery cloud hanging over the streets. The cloud was the Milky Way. Many of the callers had lived their entire lives beneath it without once seeing it.

I think about those phone calls often. They hold a parable in miniature. We have altered the night so thoroughly, and so quickly, that most of us have forgotten what it is — have gone, in a historical eyeblink, from being creatures of the dark to creatures who visit the dark, briefly, through a window. Night is half of everything. The Earth spends half of every rotation turned away from the sun, and for all but the last hundred-odd years of our species' existence, we spent that half in a darkness modern people have never experienced. What follows is an attempt to remember what that half was like: what the night used to be, what we built in its place, and what — this is the hopeful part — is still recoverable, with a switch.

[The old night]

Begin with the basics: for almost the entire human story, night was genuinely dark. Not dim. Dark. No light pollution existed... Under a new moon in open country you could not see your hand in front of your face. Travelers got lost between villages a mile apart; the moon was the only streetlamp and it kept an eccentric schedule. Light was the exception and the expense — expensive in treasure, expensive in danger. Burning flame inside a house of thatch and timber was always a small gamble.

Because night was genuinely dangerous, our ancestors organized against it. The word curfew comes from the French couvre-feu: cover the fire. In medieval towns a bell rang at a fixed hour ordering every hearth banked — a city of wooden roofs collectively exhaling its flames so everyone could sleep without the town burning down. In cities like London you could hire a link-boy, a child with a flaming torch, to walk you home through streets with no public light at all. The night had its own jurisdiction. Thieves, smugglers, and worse used it; so did the feared dead; folklore assigned the hours after midnight to spirits and the hours before dawn to melancholy.

And yet — this is what the historians emphasize — the darkness was also furnished with intimacy. Families slept in shared beds for warmth, packed like spoons with visitors and apprentices and travelers; conversation in the dark has a candor daylight doesn't allow... Firelight and storytelling; the night as the day's annex rather than its enemy.

There's an economic way to see how recently all this changed. William Nordhaus (economist who spent a career pricing light): for most of history an hour of reading by lamp cost the better part of a day's wage — in some ancient accounting, days of labor for an hour of oil-lamp light. Today an hour of electric light costs a fraction of a second of median earnings. When you hear that darkness covered most of human life, understand it as a matter of budget: the night ruled because light was unaffordable. We didn't abolish night so much as make it cheap to ignore.

[First sleep]

In 2005, the historian Roger Ekirch published "At Day's Close," a history of night in the pre-industrial West, built from years of reading diaries, letters, court records, medical texts, sermons. Reading it, you notice him tripping over the same phrase again and again: "first sleep." It appears in English, in French (premier sommeil), in Italian (primo sonno), across two millennia, always in the tone people use for things everyone knows. First sleep was the sleep you took when you went to bed not long after dark. You slept hard, deeply, for three or four hours; then around midnight you woke — not with a start but naturally, into a calm interlude that contemporaries called the watch — which might last an hour or more.

People did things in the watch. They got up and tended the fire, prayed, talked, made love — physicians of the era recommended the interval as the best time for conception — smoked a pipe, gossiped with neighbors who were also awake, checked on livestock, or simply lay still and thought, with no daylight errands to dilute the thinking. Then they went back down into second sleep until dawn.

For a long time this looked like custom. Then in the 1990s, Thomas Wehr, a sleep researcher at the National Institute of Mental Health, ran what amounted to an experiment in retrieving the old night: he gave volunteers fourteen hours of darkness each night for a month — a laboratory version of a winter. After an adjustment period, the subjects did something remarkable. Their sleep split. They slept in two blocks, waking after midnight into a quiet, dreamy, distinctly pleasant wakefulness — prolactin rising, the body in a mode no one had a name for — then slept again until "morning." The pattern Ekirch had found in five centuries of documents appeared in a lab when darkness was returned. Bimodal sleep looks less like a habit we had and more like a setting we lost.

Which casts a strange light on a modern complaint. Waking at 3 a.m., unable to return to sleep, we call it insomnia, a malfunction. It may be an echo — the watch arriving punctually in a world no longer shaped to receive it. The hour itself may not be broken. The schedule around it is.

[The conquest]

The machines that ended the night arrived quickly... Gaslight: Pall Mall in 1807; within decades, tens of thousands of burners in London and Paris, and the lamplighter with his pole became a fixture of dusk, a moving constellation at eye level. Then electricity: arc lamps like small captive suns in the 1870s-80s, then Edison's bulbs. By 1900 night, the oldest human condition, had become an infrastructure problem with a solution.

What artificial light actually invented was the evening. Before it, the hours after dark belonged to rest, talk, and courtship by candle; after it, they became a market: theaters, cafés, dance halls, cinemas, restaurants, the whole glittering secondary life of cities that now runs from 7 p.m. to 2 a.m. The city that never sleeps stopped being a boast and became a specification.

The cost was absorbed by a workforce most of us never see. Walk through any city at 4 a.m. and you will find it inhabited: bakers shaping loaves, nurses on their fourth round, stocking crews, controllers watching blips, technicians keeping water pumping and servers humming, drivers. Something like a fifth of workers in industrial countries now work nights. In 2007 the WHO's cancer research agency did something quiet and remarkable: it classified shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable human carcinogen — a formal acknowledgment that working against the body's ancient clock exacts a measurable tax. Night, once merely frightening, now has a mortality schedule.

[What we did to the sky]

Then the sky itself. In 2016, an international team led by Fabio Falchi published the first complete atlas of artificial sky brightness. Its numbers are worth sitting with: more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. For a third of humanity, the Milky Way is invisible. In Europe about 60 percent of people, and in North America about 80 percent, cannot see the galaxy they live inside.

Look at Earth from orbit at night — NASA's composite images — and you see civilization as a lace of light strung along coastlines and rivers. It's genuinely beautiful, and it is the exhaust of what we did: light escaping upward, scattering off the atmosphere into a luminous dome — skyglow — that can be detected a hundred miles from the nearest town.

Animals live inside that exhaust. Moths... For centuries the saying "like a moth to a flame" implied attraction. Slow-motion cameras have shown something stranger: insects instinctively tilt their backs toward the brightest point in view — a reflex calibrated to keep them upright beneath an open sky, with the moon overhead as a steady reference. Around a porch light, the reflex turns into a doom-loop; they circle not because they love the light but because their bodies are convinced it is the sky.

Birds: hundreds of species migrate at night, steering by stars and the earth's glow, and city lights pull them off course — collisions with buildings kill as many as a billion birds a year in the United States. A famous experiment in accidental astronomy: the 9/11 Tribute in Light in Manhattan drew migrating birds into orbit inside the beams at enormous rates; researchers persuaded the organizers to douse the lights for twenty minutes, and the birds dispersed almost immediately — the machinery of their confusion simply switched off.

Sea turtles: hatchlings emerge at night and orient toward the brighter horizon — on a wild beach, moonlight and starlight on water; on a developed one, a resort. Towns in Florida now pass beach lighting ordinances each hatching season, dimming and shielding lights so hatchlings can find the ocean instead of the parking lot. Plants, too: a Swiss study found that meadow plots lit at night by ordinary LED lamps received nearly two-thirds fewer visits from pollinating insects — and the plants set less fruit. Night is not empty. Darkness is not the absence of habitat; it is habitat, for a large fraction of the living world, and we have been paving it the way we pave wetlands, without noticing, because it doesn't look like anything.

[The night mind]

And us. Why does 3 a.m. have its reputation? Partly mechanics: the prefrontal cortex is tired, no news arrives, no errands interrupt, no one is awake to reality-check you; rumination gets the whole room. Anxieties that daylight dilutes concentrate in the dark like sediment in a glass. Every insomniac knows the special physics of the 3 a.m. problem: it is always larger at night, and by morning it has shrunk back to size, as though daylight were a solvent.

But night also does stranger and kinder work. Mary Shelley was eighteen in 1816, the year without a summer, holed up on Lake Geneva with Byron and her husband and ghost stories by candlelight, when she described falling into a waking dream — the pale student, the thing stirring on the table — that became Frankenstein. Kekulé claimed the structure of benzene arrived in a dream of a snake seizing its own tail. (Maybe.) The unconscious keeps the night shift; it takes the problems we fall asleep on and returns them rearranged. Night thought is not defective day thought. It is a different instrument — looser, less defended — and some of what our species has made appeared first in that other room.

[Taking the night back]

Here is the good news, and it is rare in environmental news of any kind: this particular damage reverses at the speed of a switch. Air and water pollution take decades and fortune to undo; light pollution ends when the light ends. The dark-sky movement — DarkSky International and its certified places — has mapped this out in practice. Central Idaho contains a certified dark sky reserve the size of a small country. On the Isle of Coll, off Scotland, the whole community agreed to manage its lighting so visitors can see the Milky Way from a football pitch. Tucson, Arizona, sits near some of the great observatories in the world, and decades ago the city rewrote its lighting code — full shielding, warm bulbs, light pointed at the ground where it's useful instead of the sky where it isn't — and the observatories kept their view. None of these places is poorer or darker for it; they simply buy their light the way earlier generations had to, on purpose.

And at personal scale: it takes about twenty minutes of true darkness for human eyes to reach full sensitivity — a dilation you can feel happening, the world slowly assembling itself out of fainter and fainter signals. Guides at dark-sky parks report a curious thing: visitors who see the Milky Way for the first time go quiet, and some of them cry. Not only, I think, at the beauty — a river of several hundred billion suns visible to the naked eye — but at the return of something. Grief and gratitude feel similar at first.

Which brings us back to Los Angeles in 1994. The silvery cloud over the blacked-out city had been there the whole time, above the traffic and the billboards, the whole time. It took a catastrophe to show people what they had, in effect, turned off — or rather, what they still had and couldn't see. There is a version of that blackout available in miniature. Our ancestors woke in the watch and lay in the dark between first sleep and second sleep, unbothered, watching embers, thinking their long thoughts, sometimes stepping outside into a sky absolutely stiff with stars. Some of us still wake in that hour and reach, first thing, for a small bright screen — colonizing the last of the night even from bed. The invitation misdelivered might be read another way. You are not malfunctioning; you may be punctual. The night was never the other half of the world. It is the half we came from, and it is still there, patient, just above the streetlights, waiting for the switch.
